title: 2012_PMC3469560_Attitudes_of_the_general_public_and_general_practitioners_in_fiv
ehr_evidence: In December 2009/January 2010 and April 2010, 500 randomly selected members of the general public in Germany, France, the United States, China, and Mexico were surveyed by telephone about vaccination for seasonal and A/H1N1 pandemic influenza; GPs participated via a computer-assisted web interview.
summary: A cross-sectional telephone/web survey of 500 general public members and 100 general practitioners per country in France, Germany, the US, China, and Mexico examining whether the 2009/2010 A/H1N1 pandemic affected seasonal influenza vaccine uptake and attitudes.
key_findings: Adult A/H1N1 pandemic vaccine coverage in December 2009/January 2010 was 41% in the US versus approximately 10-13% in France, Germany, Mexico, and China.
The 2009/2010 A/H1N1 pandemic increased seasonal influenza vaccine uptake only in Mexico (adult VCR rose from 30% to 46%), with little or no effect in France, Germany, the US, and China.
Physician advice or recommendation was the most common reason for receiving the pandemic vaccine in France, Germany, and Mexico.
Inclusion of the A/H1N1 pandemic strain increased willingness to be vaccinated for seasonal influenza in the US, Mexico, and China but not in Germany or France.
More than 90% of respondents in France and Germany perceived the A/H1N1 threat as mild to moderate (mean score <5), versus 51% in Mexico perceiving it as serious (mean score 6.9).
captured_features: vaccination coverage rates (A/H1N1 and seasonal) by age group and country
perceived threat/risk severity of A/H1N1 influenza (0-10 scale)
intention to be vaccinated next season
population: adults (≥18 years) from the general public and general practitioners in France, Germany, the US, China, and Mexico
exposure_domain: pandemic influenza (A/H1N1) and seasonal influenza vaccination
limitations: Low survey response rates (e.g., 5-7% in France and Germany) with possible selection bias.
Small sample size of 500 public members and 100 GPs per country.
Vaccination coverage relied on respondents' recollection and honesty (recall bias).
Only the three largest cities were sampled in China and Mexico, potentially overestimating coverage.
Self-reported data with respondents aware of being surveyed.
